title: Indexes: why your query is slow

claims.text: Bayer and McCreight addressed the organisation and maintenance of an index for a dynamic random access file, assuming the index must be kept on a backup store such as a disc, in Acta Informatica in 1972, volume 1, pages 173 to 189. Their organisation allows retrieval, insertion and deletion of keys in time proportional to the logarithm of the index size, with the base being a device-dependent number, and storage utilisation of at least fifty percent.

source.title: R. Bayer and E. M. McCreight, Organization and maintenance of large ordered indexes, Acta Informatica 1(3):173-189, 1972, doi 10.1007/BF00288683

claims.text: The structure they name is organised so that each node holds many keys rather than one: in a tree of order k each node contains at most 2k keys and 2k+1 pointers and at least k keys, so each node is at least half full. Their experiments ran with indexes up to one hundred thousand keys, maintaining an index of fifteen thousand at an average of nine transactions per second on the hardware of the day.

source.title: R. Bayer and E. M. McCreight, Organization and maintenance of large ordered indexes, Acta Informatica 1(3):173-189, 1972, doi 10.1007/BF00288683

beats.broke: answering a question about one row means examining every row, and the rows live on a device where each access costs a fixed and enormous delay regardless of how little you read
beats.fix: keep an ordered structure beside the data whose nodes are sized to the device's block, so that each access read from the device eliminates most of the remaining candidates rather than one of them
beats.cost: the structure has to be maintained on every write, so every index makes insertion, update and deletion slower and consumes storage, which is why they are chosen rather than created by default
beats.interview: why an index makes reads faster and what it makes slower
